·
1 1. Course map, sources, and how to use this manual
History of Uzbekistan, code CC-MOHU010106, Tashkent University of Technology,
Faculty of Energy. Compulsory module, 4 ECTS, Fall semester 2026/2027; coordina-
tor — Dr Vohid Kholov. Workload: 30 contact hours of lectures (2 hours per week,
15 weeks) + 90 hours of independent work = 120 hours. Assessment: midterm exam
— written, 1–2 hours, 30% (ILO 1-5); project presentation — written and oral, 10–15
minutes, 20%; final exam — written, 1–2 hours, 50%. Grading scale: 90 −100 = A
(excellent), 75 −89 = B(good), 60 −74 = C(satisfactory), 0 −59 = D(unsatisfactory); a
minimum of 75% attendance is required to be admitted to the final exam.
Intended Learning Outcomes (ILO): (1) Understanding — explain basic concepts of
history, statehood, and the role of science and technology in the country’s develop-
ment; (2) Analysis — analyze contemporary Uzbek politics in retrospect; (3) Selec-
tion — select qualitative and quantitative data and methods (Orientalism, oral his-
tory, source analysis, hermeneutics); (4) Evaluation — judge political changes and
reforms: openness and transparency, multi-vector foreign policy, socially-oriented
policy; (5) Application — work in small groups on projects and present historical
processes in writing and orally.
This manual covers weeks 5–6 — two thematic blocks: ”National Legislation and Ju-
dicial Systems” (creation of the 1992 Constitution, history of criminal courts from the
Avesta to the 20th century, the judicial system of the Uzbek SSR in 1939–1945, four
stages of legal system development) and ”Human Rights and Elimination of Forced
Labor” (ILO conventions No. 29 and No. 105, national labor legislation, institutional
mechanisms, child labor in the cotton industry). Sources — 6 scientific articles of the
course; all facts, dates, and figures are taken from them verbatim, quotes are given
in Russian translation with authors indicated.
How to use the manual: (1) start with the ”Key Points” section of each week — this is
the ”all rules” of the week in a condensed form; (2) solve the open questions (savollar)
aloud, covering the answers, and check against the model answers; (3) take the tests
(testlar); (4) learn the glossary atamalar — terms appear in definition questions and
in tests; (5) before the exam, review the table of dates and numbers from chapter 5
”Cheat Sheet”.

2 2. Week 5 — National Legislation and Judicial Systems
Week files: history-of-the-creation-of-the-constitution-of-the-republic-of-uzbekistan (Sh. Buron)· pcad-
min_163 (G. Yusupjanova —
criminal courts)· pcadmin_28 (D. Komilov — courts during the Great Patriotic War)· pcadmmin_39 (N.
Azizov — legal system)
Week 5 addresses the questions: how the first Constitution of independent Uzbek-
istan (1992) was created and what it established; how criminal courts developed in
the territory of the country—from the ”Avesta” and khanates through Turkestan and
the Soviet system to the present day; how the judicial system of the Uzbek SSR func-
tioned in 1939–1945 and what four stages the legal system of the independent state
has gone through. Below are the key provisions, questions (savollar), tests (testlar),
and terms (atamalar) for the four articles of the week.
2.1 2.1. Key provisions (”all the rules” of the week)
Creation of the Constitution: commission, world experience and concepts
The idea of a new Constitution was born together with the Declaration of Indepen-
dence of June 20, 1990: the session of the Supreme Council that adopted it decided to
develop a constitution and created a Constitutional Commission of 64 people headed
by the first President I. A. Karimov (on July 2–3, 1992, the composition was updated
to 71 members). The meeting of April 12, 1991, launched direct work: a working
group of 32 people and 6 small groups with the participation of 50 researchers were
formed—on the preamble, foundations of the constitutional system, rights and obli-
gations of citizens, society and the individual, state structure, state power, and final
provisions. Constitutions of the USA, Germany, France, Turkey, Japan, Lithuania and
other countries, as well as draft constitutions of seven CIS republics, were studied in
depth. Of the three alternative concepts, the concept of the President’s rule of law
(article by Sh. Buronov) was adopted as the basis.
Versions of the draft: from 158 articles to 127
The first version was ready by October–November 1991—158 articles, six sections;
the most important impulse was the constitutional law ”On the Foundations of State
Independence” of August 31, 1991. In the spring of 1992, a second version of 149
articles appeared, followed by a third—of 137; for nationwide discussion, a text of
127 articles was published. The draft was initially compiled in Russian, and in July–
August 1992 it was translated into Uzbek. Each version was read personally and
3

History of Uzbekistan · Weeks 5–6
·
corrected by hand by the chairman of the commission: ”The President... read the
draft again and again, carefully followed the text and made corrections to it,” recalled
Academician Sh. Z. Orazaev (article by Sh. Buronov).
Nationwide discussion in two stages
September 5, 1992, the Constitutional Commission comprehensively discussed the
draft, and on September 26 it was published in the press.
The discussion—from
late September to early December 1992—took place in newspapers, on radio and
television, in collectives and student classrooms; letters were sent by scientists and
pensioners, workers and dehkans, military and religious figures. More than 6,000
proposals and comments were received, the commission alone received more than
a thousand letters; corrections were made to 60 of the 127 articles, 4 articles were
excluded, several new ones were added. On November 21, 1992, the draft was pub-
lished a second time—a legal precedent of a two-stage nationwide discussion was
created. The author calls the adopted Basic Law a truly ”people’s law” (article by
Sh. Buronov).
Adoption of the Constitution on December 8, 1992 and its key norms
December 8, 1992, the eleventh session of the Supreme Council adopted the
Constitution—the Basic Law of the Republic of Uzbekistan, which legally formalized
the new sovereign democratic state. Deputies made about 80 changes and clarifica-
tions: the term of office of the Constitutional, Supreme, and Higher Economic
Courts was reduced from ten to five years; Art. 42 was adopted in a new version—
on the freedom of scientific and technical creativity; at the suggestion of deputy
Khalimakhon Usmanova, ”Motherhood and childhood are under the protection of
the state” was added to Art. 64 (now 65).
Based on the proposals of the chairman of the commission, Art. 26 (presumption of
innocence), Art. 27 (secrecy of correspondence and telephone conversations) and
Art. 31—freedom of conscience: ”The forced imposition of religious views is not per-
mitted” were consolidated. The Arbitration Court was transformed into an Economic
Court, and the parliament was named the Oliy Majlis. The commission rejected a
bicameral structure, mandatory union membership, and the appointment of prose-
cutors with the consent of khokims (article by Sh. Buronov).
Justice of antiquity and the Middle Ages: from the ”Avesta” to the khanates
Already in the ”Avesta” — one of the ancient cultural and legal sources of the region
— there were rules concerning judicial cases: the court determined guilt, the valid-
ity of the claim, and punishment. The Saka, Kangju, Huns, Sarmatians, Karluk and
Turkic Khaganates had their own legal systems, often based on prejudices. Accord-
ing to Muslim law, crimes were classified from religious and ideological positions,
and a single judge handled all criminal and family-inheritance cases. In the Bukhara
and Khiva Khanates, the heads of the judicial authority were emirs and khans: they
conducted public proceedings — mainly concerning non-payment of taxes, plunder
of the treasury, and rebellions. Only the khan could pass a death sentence; the kush-
begi, beks, qazi-kalon (supreme judge) and qazi-askar (military judge) had all rights
”except the right of life and death” (according to the article by G. Yusupdzhanova).
The judicial system of Turkestan in the Russian Empire (1865–1917)
After the conquest of Central Asia, the colonial authorities established a court ac-
cording to the laws of the empire. The ”Temporary Provision” of 1865 defined the
procedure for introducing Russian justice; the ”Draft Provision on the Organization
4


History of Uzbekistan · Weeks 5–6
·
of the Judicial Branch” of 1867 (in three parts) introduced a two-tier imperial sys-
tem; the ”Provision on the Administration of the Turkestan Region” approved by the
emperor on June 12, 1886, became the main legal document of the region. General
courts and courts based on sharia operated in parallel; for the nomadic population,
the courts of qadis and bays were preserved. The district judge combined the con-
sideration of minor cases with preliminary investigation. The reforms of 1897–1899
created a judicial chamber — the highest instance with control functions; concilia-
tory judges (district, additional, honorary) could arrest for up to three days. The
fourth stage (1898–1917) adapted the system to the Judicial Statutes of the empire
(article by G. Yusupdzhanova).
Soviet criminal courts: 1917–1960
The December 1917 decree suspended district courts, the Tashkent judicial cham-
ber, and military courts; people’s courts, tribunals, and revolutionary tribunals ap-
peared, punishing those unsympathetic to the Bolshevik ideology. Under pressure
from public protests, the Soviets preserved the courts of qadis and bays: in 1922,
the ”Provision on the Court of Qadis of the Turkestan Republic” was adopted, and on
August 1, 1922, the first systematic Code of Criminal Procedure came into force. The
1926 Code of Criminal Procedure established judicial control over detention and case
dismissal (arts. 201, 202, 244); the 1929 Code simplified the procedure but allowed
the court to draw up the indictment itself. Based on the ”Fundamentals of Criminal
Justice of the USSR” of 1958, a new Code of Criminal Procedure of the Uzbek SSR
was approved on May 21, 1959, and introduced into practice on January 1, 1960
(article by G. Yusupdzhanova).
Law of 1938 on the Judicial System and Court Personnel of the Uzbek SSR
(1937-1939)
On August 16, 1938, the second session of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR adopted
the Law ”On the Judicial System of the USSR, Union and Autonomous Republics” —
8 chapters and 80 articles based on the Constitution of the USSR of 1936. Courts
were divided into all-Union (Supreme Court of the USSR, military tribunals, railway
and water transport courts) and courts of the Union republics. People’s judges were
elected by citizens of the district for 3 years; regional and Supreme Courts — for 5
years. In the second half of 1939, in the Uzbek SSR, there were 226 people’s courts,
five regional courts, and the Surkhandarya District Court.
The personnel were weak: out of 225 people’s judges, only 17 had higher education.
In 1937-1939, 541 judges were dismissed, only 6 people’s judges completed their
full term — 2.6%. People’s Commissar of Justice D. Turdiev recorded the collusion
of judges with criminals, and people’s courts were housed in unsuitable buildings —
mosques and warehouses; for Judge Inoyatov, half of the decisions and most of the
verdicts were overturned (article by D. Komolov).
The judicial system of the Uzbek SSR during the years of the Second World
War (1941–1945)
On June 22, 1941, on the day of Germany’s invasion, the regulations ”On the State
of War” and ”On Military Tribunals” were adopted: the trial had to begin within 24
hours after the accused was brought to trial, the death sentence was announced
after 72 hours, cassation was prohibited — the sentence was changed only in the
supervisory procedure. In 1942, the Tashkent Railway and Water Transport Court
was transformed into a military tribunal.
The decree of July 15, 1941 reduced staffing levels: judges’ leaves were canceled, the
network of people’s courts was cut by 20% in rural areas and 25% in cities; in 1942,
5

·
28 people’s courts were closed. The personnel shortage was addressed through edu-
cation: the Tashkent Law Institute, suspended in 1941, resumed operations in 1942,
and in August 1943, four-month courses were opened in Tashkent and six-month
courses in Samarkand. By the end of 1945, only 56 lawyers with higher education
remained in the people’s courts (article by D. Komolov).
Four stages in the development of the legal system of independent Uzbek-
istan
N. P. Azizov identifies four stages. The first (1991–2000) — transitional period and
formation of the foundations of national statehood: constitutional law of August 31,
1991 (17 articles), Constitution, new branches of law, 15 codes from 1994–2008. The
second (2001–2009) — democratic renewal: bicameral parliament, abolition of the
death penalty and transfer of arrest sanctions to the courts (2007), reclassification of
75% of serious crimes as less serious, and 20% fewer sentences by 2006 compared
to 2000.
Third (2010–2016) — deepening of democratic reforms (about fifty laws).
Fourth
(since 2017) — Strategy of Actions: judicial reform — second priority; the Supreme
Council of Judges and the unified Supreme Court were created, 71 economic courts,
judges — first for 5, then for 10 years and for life; torture is prohibited. Sh. Mirziy-
oyev: ”Ensuring the genuine independence of the judiciary is our number one pri-
ority” (quoted from D. Komolov). In Lex.uz — 99,706 documents (article by N. P.
Azizov).
2.2 2.2. Savollar — questions of articles and model answers
S1. When, by what body and in what context was the first Constitution of the
Republic of Uzbekistan adopted?
Answer. The Constitution was adopted on December 8, 1992 by the eleventh ses-
sion of the Supreme Council of the Republic of Uzbekistan. It legally formalized the
formation of a new sovereign democratic state — the Republic of Uzbekistan — on
the political world map and, according to the author of the article, was created as
the fruit and product of state independence. At the session itself, deputies made
about 80 amendments, additions, and clarifications. The first President I. A. Kari-
mov, who chaired the Constitutional Commission, called the basic law ”a manifesto
of our freedom and security” (article by Sh. Buronov).
S2. How was the Constitutional Commission formed and how did it work?
Answer. After the adoption of the Declaration of Independence (June 20, 1990), a
session of the Supreme Council created a commission of 64 people chaired by I.
A. Karimov; on July 2–3, 1992, the composition was updated to 71 members. The
meeting of April 12, 1991, began direct work: a working group of 32 people and
6 small groups (50 researchers) were created for the sections of the draft project.
Constitutions of the USA, Germany, France, Japan, Lithuania and other states, and
draft constitutions of seven CIS republics were studied; of three alternative concepts,
the concept of the President’s rule of law (article by Sh. Buronov) was adopted as
the basis.
S3. What versions did the draft Constitution go through before publication?
Answer. The first version (October–November 1991) contained 158 articles in six
sections; in the spring of 1992, the second was prepared—149 articles, then the
third—137 articles. For nationwide discussion, a version of 127 articles was pub-
lished. The project was initially prepared in Russian; in July–August 1992, at the
6


History of Uzbekistan · Weeks 5–6
·
direction of the head of the working group Sh. Z. Orazayev, the text was translated
into Uzbek. Each version was carefully studied and edited by the chairman of the
commission (article by Sh. Buronov).
S4. How did the nationwide discussion of the draft Constitution proceed?
Answer.
On September 5, 1992, the commission comprehensively discussed the
project, and on September 26 it was published in the press. The discussion—from
late September to early December 1992—took place in the press, on radio and tele-
vision, in labor collectives and student auditoriums; more than 6,000 proposals and
comments and more than a thousand letters were received. Corrections were made
to 60 of the 127 articles, 4 articles were excluded. On November 21, 1992, the project
was published a second time—a precedent of two-stage discussion was established.
The author calls the Constitution a ”people’s law” (article by Sh. Buronov).
S5.
What key norms were included in the Constitution as a result of the
discussion?
Answer. At the chairman’s proposal, the following were included: Art. 26 — pre-
sumption of innocence; Art. 27 — secrecy of correspondence and telephone conver-
sations; Art. 31 — freedom of conscience (”Everyone has the right to believe in any
religion or not to believe in any. The forced imposition of religious views is not per-
mitted”). The Arbitration Court was transformed into an Economic Court, and the
parliament was named the Oliy Majlis. At the deputy Khalimakhon Usmonova’s pro-
posal, ”Motherhood and childhood are under the protection of the state” was added
to Art. 64 (now 65) (article by Sh. Buronov).
S6. What proposals were rejected during the preparation and adoption of
the Constitution?
Answer. The commission rejected the proposal for a bicameral Oliy Majlis (Chamber
of Representatives and Chamber of Nations) — the idea of bicameralism was only
returned to later, during the second convocation. At the meeting on December 7,
1992, the norm on the suspension of the President’s party membership was excluded
(draft Art. 90). Membership in trade unions was not supported (contrary to the vol-
untary nature of associations) and the appointment of prosecutors with the consent
of khokims: the prosecutor’s office is built on the principle of unity of command, all
prosecutors are appointed by the Prosecutor General (article by Sh. Buronov).
S7. How was justice administered in ancient times and in the Bukhara and
Khiva Khanates?
Answer. Already in the ”Avesta” there are rules about judicial cases: the court de-
termined the guilt of the perpetrator, the validity of the claim and the punishment.
Among the Sakas, Kangyue, Huns, Sarmatians, Karluk and Turkic Khaganates, their
own legal systems operated. According to Muslim law, a single judge handled all
criminal and family-inheritance cases. In the khanates, the head of the judicial power
was the emir and khan; only the khan could pass a death sentence, while the kush-
begi, beks, qazi-kalon and qazi-askar had rights ”except the right to life and death”
(article by G. Yusupdzhanova).
S8. What judicial system did the Russian Empire introduce in Turkestan?
Answer. The ”Temporary Provision” of 1865 defined the procedure for introducing
imperial justice; the ”Draft Provision” of 1867 introduced a two-tier court system;
the ”Provision on the Administration of the Turkestan Region”, approved by the em-
peror on June 12, 1886, became the main legal document. General courts and courts
based on Sharia operated in parallel; for the nomadic population, the courts of qazis
and biys were preserved. The district judge performed a dual function — he con-
7

·
sidered minor cases and conducted preliminary investigation. The reforms of 1897-
1899 created a judicial chamber — the highest instance of the region (article by G.
Yusupdzhanova).
S9. How did criminal courts change during the Soviet period (1917-1960)?
Answer. The December 1917 decree suspended district courts, the Tashkent judicial
chamber and military courts; people’s courts, tribunals and revolutionary tribunals
appeared, punishing those unsympathetic to Bolshevism. In 1922, a document on
the courts of qazis was adopted, and on August 1, 1922, the first systematicized
Code of Criminal Procedure was introduced.
The Code of Criminal Procedure of
the Uzbek SSR of 1926 consolidated judicial control over preventive measures and
termination of cases; the Code of Criminal Procedure of 1929 simplified the process
but allowed the court to draw up an indictment. According to the ”Fundamentals
of Criminal Justice of the USSR” of 1958, a new Code of Criminal Procedure was
approved on May 21, 1959, which came into force on January 1, 1960 (article by G.
Yusupdzhanova).
S10. What did the Law ”On the Judicial System” of August 16, 1938 establish?
Answer. The law consisted of 8 chapters and 80 articles and was developed on the ba-
sis of the Constitution of the USSR of 1936. The courts were divided into two groups:
all-Union (Supreme Court of the USSR, military tribunals, railway and water trans-
port courts) and courts of the union republics (people’s, regional, Supreme Courts
of the autonomous and union republic). People’s judges were elected by citizens of
the district for 3 years (a citizen from 23 years of age could be elected); regional
and Supreme Courts — for 5 years. At the Supreme Court of the USSR, a Plenum
operated, which met no less than once every two months (article by D. Komolov).
S11. What was the staffing situation of the courts of the Uzbek SSR on the
eve of the war?
Answer. In the second half of 1939, 226 people’s courts were operating in the Uzbek
SSR (only one was closed—due to a shortage of specialists); of the 225 people’s
judges, 17 had higher education, and 46 were women. In 1937-1939, 541 judges
were dismissed; only 6 people’s judges served their full term (2.6%). There were
five regional courts (Tashkent, Samarkand, Fergana, Khorezm, Bukhara) plus the
Surkhandarya District Court with 68 judges. People’s Commissar of Justice D. Tur-
diev recorded cases of collusion between judges and criminals; courts were housed
in mosques and warehouses (article by D. Komolov).
S12. How did military tribunals work during the war?
Answer. According to the regulation of June 22, 1941, the trial was appointed within
24 hours after the accused was brought to trial, the death sentence was announced
within 72 hours, and cassation appeals were prohibited—the verdict could only be
changed in the supervisory procedure. Until 1943, tribunals consisted of three per-
manent members without people’s assessors; their members were not elected but ap-
pointed by joint orders of the People’s Commissariats of Justice and Defense. Cases
were heard mainly behind closed doors. The execution could be postponed until the
end of combat operations—the convicted ”washed away their guilt with blood” at the
front, some were then acquitted and awarded (article by D. Komolov).
S13. How did the war change courts of general jurisdiction and the training
of legal personnel?
Answer. The decree of July 15, 1941 reduced staffing: judges’ leaves were canceled,
people’s courts were cut by 20% in rural areas and 25% in cities; in 1942, 28 peo-
ple’s courts were closed in the republic. Mobilization affected 20–30% of judges in
8


History of Uzbekistan · Weeks 5–6
·
some regions (in Fergana—8 out of 24 people’s judges). The personnel shortage was
addressed through courses: the Tashkent Law Institute resumed operations in 1942,
in August 1943, four-month courses were opened in Tashkent and six-month courses
in Samarkand; by January 1, 1944, 40 people’s judges had completed internships. By
the end of 1945, only 56 lawyers with higher education remained in people’s courts
(article by D. Komolov).
S14.
What stages of the development of the legal system of independent
Uzbekistan does N. P. Azizov identify?
Answer. Four stages: (1) 1991–2000 — transitional period and formation of the foun-
dations of national statehood (Declaration of Independence, constitutional law of Au-
gust 31, 1991 with 17 articles, Constitution; for 1994–2008 — 15 codes); (2) 2001–
2009 — democratic renewal: bicameral parliament, abolition of the death penalty
and transfer of arrest sanctions to courts (2007); (3) 2010–2016 — implementation
of the Concept of Deepening Democratic Reforms (about fifty laws); (4) from 2017
— Action Strategy 2017–2021: Supreme Council of Judges, merger of the Supreme
and Higher Economic Courts, 71 economic courts, prohibition of torture (article by
N. P. Azizov).
S15. What mechanisms for involving citizens in lawmaking appeared in the
fourth stage?
Answer. According to the President’s Address of December 23, 2017, the ”My Opin-
ion” collective appeals portal was launched: 440 collective appeals were published.
On the portal for discussing draft normative legal acts of the Ministry of Justice,
about 8,000 acts were considered, including 557 bills and 2,380 draft government
resolutions, with about 35,000 proposals submitted. For youth (under 18 years old
— about 40% of the population, under 30 years old — 64%), a ”Youth Parliament”
was created under the Legislative Chamber; on June 29, 2020, an agreement was
signed with the Central Council of the Youth Union. On February 27, 2020, a Parlia-
mentary Commission for monitoring the Sustainable Development Goals until 2030
was established (article by N. P. Azizov).
2.3 2.3. Testlar — tests with correct answers
T1. When was the first Constitution of the Republic of Uzbekistan adopted?
a) August 31, 1991 b) June 20, 1990 c) December 8, 1992 d) November 21, 1992
Answer: c) December 8, 1992
Explanation: According to Sh. Buronov’s article, the Constitution was adopted at the
eleventh session of the Supreme Council on December 8, 1992; August 31, 1991 is the
date of the law on the foundations of independence, June 20, 1990 is the Declaration
of Independence, and November 21, 1992 is the republication of the draft.
T2. How many people initially joined the Constitutional Commission under
the chairmanship of I. A. Karimov?
a) 32 b) 64 c) 71 d) 50 Answer: b) 64
Note: A commission of 64 people was established by the session that adopted the
Declaration of Independence; on July 2–3, 1992, the composition was updated to 71
members; 32 — working group, 50 — researchers of small groups (article by Sh.
Buronov).
T3. How many articles did the first draft of the Constitution, prepared for
October–November 1991, contain?
a) 127 b) 137 c) 149 d) 158 Answer: d) 158
9

History of Uzbekistan · Weeks 5–6
·
Note: The first version — 158 articles in six sections; then 149, 137 and 127 articles
(version for public discussion) — article by Sh. Buronov.
T4. Who in the Bukhara and Khiva Khanates could pass a death sentence?
a) qazi-kalon b) only the khan (emir) c) kushbegi d) qazi-askar Answer: b) only the
khan (emir)
Note: According to the article by G. Yusupdzhanova, the kushbegi, beks, qazi-kalon
(supreme judge) and qazi-askar (military judge) had all rights ”except the right to life
and death”; for the death penalty, the permission of the khan (emir) was required.
T5. When was the ”Regulation on the Administration of the Turkestan Re-
gion” — the main legal document of the region — approved by the emperor?
a) in 1865 b) in 1867 c) June 12, 1886 d) in 1897 Answer: c) June 12, 1886
Explanation: ”The Temporary Provision” refers to 1865, ”The Draft Provision on the
Organization of the Judicial Part” refers to 1867, the third stage of reforms refers
to 1897; the ”Provision” itself was approved on June 12, 1886 (according to G.
Yusupdzhanova’s article).
T6. When was the Code of Criminal Procedure of the Uzbek SSR, approved
on May 21, 1959, introduced into legal practice?
a) May 21, 1959 b) August 1, 1922 c) January 1, 1960 d) in 1958 Answer: c) January
1, 1960
Explanation: According to G. Yusupdzhanova’s article, the law approving the code
was adopted on May 21, 1959, based on the ”Fundamentals of Criminal Justice of
the USSR” of 1958, and the code was introduced into practice on January 1, 1960.
T7. How many chapters and articles did the Law ”On the Judicial System of
the USSR, Union and Autonomous Republics” of 1938 contain?
a) 8 chapters and 80 articles b) 6 chapters and 64 articles c) 12 chapters and 100
articles d) 10 chapters and 58 articles Answer: a) 8 chapters and 80 articles
Explanation: The law, adopted on August 16, 1938, based on the Constitution of the
USSR of 1936, consisted of 8 chapters and 80 articles (according to D. Komolov’s
article).
T8. For what term was a people’s judge elected according to the 1938 law?
a) for 5 years b) for 3 years c) for 10 years d) for 2 years Answer: b) for 3 years
Explanation: According to Article 22 of the law (cited by D. Komolov), people’s judges
are elected for 3 years, starting from age 23; five years is the term for regional and
Supreme Courts; ten years is the term of office of the courts, reduced by the 1992
Constitution to five.
T9. How many people’s courts were operating in the Uzbek SSR in the second
half of 1939?
a) 68 b) 225 c) 226 d) 28 Answer: c) 226
Explanation: According to D. Komolov’s article — 226 people’s courts (one closed
due to lack of specialists); 225 is the number of people’s judges, 68 is the number of
regional and district court judges, 28 is the number of courts reduced in 1942.
T10. Within what time after being brought to trial should the process begin
in a military tribunal?
a) within 72 hours b) within 24 hours c) within five days d) within one month Answer:

Week 6 answers the questions: what is forced labor according to ILO Conventions
No. 29 and No. 105 and how Uzbekistan has implemented international standards;
what institutional mechanisms to combat forced labor have been formed since 1992;
why child labor became systemic in the cotton sector, what are its scale, conditions
and consequences, and how the state and international community responded. Below
are the key provisions, savollar, testlar and atamalar for the two articles of the week.
3.1 3.1. Key provisions (”all rules” of the week)
Forced labor: definition and ILO Conventions No. 29 and No. 105
According to ILO estimates (2017), 40.3 million people are in modern slavery: 24.9
million — in forced labor, 15.4 million — in forced marriage; every fourth victim is
a child. Convention No. 29 (1930) defines: ”Forced or compulsory labour means all
work or service which is exacted from any person under the threat of any penalty
and to which he has not offered himself voluntarily.” The definition is based on four
elements: work or service; any person; involuntary nature; threat of penalty. Art. 2
of the Convention excludes military service, ordinary civic obligations, work under
court sentence, emergencies, and minor community works from the concept.
Convention No. 105 (1957) requires the immediate abolition of forced labor in five
cases: as a means of political coercion or punishment for political opinions; as a
method of labor mobilization for economic development; as a means of labor disci-
pline; as punishment for participation in strikes; as a means of racial, social, national
or religious discrimination.
Uzbekistan and international labor standards
As of January 1, 2021, Uzbekistan had ratified 17 ILO conventions (including 8 fun-
damental ones) and 1 protocol: conventions Nos. 29 and 105, the 2014 Protocol to
Convention No. 29 (ratified on June 25, 2019, and entered into force for Uzbekistan
12


History of Uzbekistan · Weeks 5–6
·
on September 16, 2020), convention No. 182 on the worst forms of child labor and
No. 138 on the minimum age. The 1966 UN covenants on civil and political rights
and on economic, social and cultural rights have also been ratified.
The head of
the delegation to the 103rd session of the International Labour Conference, T. Nar-
baeva, emphasized: ”Ratification of conventions is only 50 percent of the solution to
the problem,” the rest is the implementation of norms and changing the mindset of
farmers and employers (article by O. Sulyaimanov and J. Rasulov).
Prohibition of forced labor in national legislation
Article 37 of the Constitution prohibits forced labor, except for serving a sentence by
court order and other cases provided for by law. Article 10 of the Labor Code allows
for the direct application of ratified conventions; article 7 defines forced labor as
”the performance of work under the threat of any penalty (including as a means of
maintaining labor discipline).” The authors note a defect: the element of voluntary
non-offering of services has been excluded from the national definition, due to which
coercion outside of labor relations may not fall under the norm. Responsibility is
established by Art. 1482 of the Criminal Code and Art. 51 of the Administrative
Code — but only for ”administrative coercion to labor”; it is proposed to extend it to
any persons (article by O. Sulyaimanov and J. Rasulov).
Khoshar: voluntary labor and exceptions to the concept of forced labor
Uzbek legislation uses a single term ”forced labor” (majburiy mehnat).
A special
place is occupied by the institution of khoshar: the dictionary defines it as ”voluntary,
selfless participation of the majority in completing a task.” The Resolution of the
Cabinet of Ministers of May 10, 2018, No. 349 allows for the involvement in public
works, including construction and agricultural, only on a voluntary basis and with
the presence of the corresponding document of the President or resolution of the
Cabinet of Ministers; greening and improvement works can be organized without
strict permission. Coercion to khoshar under the threat of punishment is a direct
sign of forced labor; the authors propose to enshrine in the law a legal definition of
khoshar (article by O. Sulyaimanov and J. Rasulov).
Three periods of formation of institutional mechanisms
First period (1992–2007): Uzbekistan joined the ILO, ratified conventions Nos. 29
and 105, adopted the Labor Code and the Employment Law, created state labor in-
spections; no special structures existed yet. Second period (2008–2016): interna-
tional organizations reported on the systematic use of forced and child labor; conven-
tions Nos. 182 and 138 and the UN protocol on trafficking in persons were ratified,
the Law ”On Combating Trafficking in Persons” and resolutions Nos. 207, 82, 132
were adopted; an interdepartmental commission and a Rehabilitation Center were
created; in 2013 — the Coordinating Council on Child Labor.
Third period (since 2017): criminal liability for forced labor was established, special
mechanisms were formed, cooperation with the ILO was resumed — a Parliamentary
Commission (Senate resolution of October 4, 2017, No. SQ-231-III), a Republican
interdepartmental commission (resolution of May 31, 2018, No. 407), a tripartite
commission (resolution of July 3, 2019, No. 553), a National Commission and an
Institute of the National Rapporteur (decree PF-5775 of July 30, 2019).
Three types of mechanisms and national monitoring
Today, three types of mechanisms are in operation: (1) collegial bodies — the National
Commission on Combating Trafficking in Persons and Forced Labor, the Coordination
13

History of Uzbekistan · Weeks 5–6
·
Council on Child Labor, the Republican Tripartite Commission on Social and Labor
Issues; (2) labor authorities — state labor inspectorates (Resolution No.
1066 of
December 31, 2018), authorized to initiate cases and transfer materials to court; (3)
civil society institutions — trade unions and NGOs. In 2019, 259 cases of forced labor
were identified, fines under Art. 51 of the Code of Administrative Offenses amounted
to 772 million sum, of which 141 cases were in cotton harvesting.
According to
the National Commission, for the 2020 cotton campaign, 42 officials (including the
khokim and his deputies) were held accountable; in another 6 cases, documents were
submitted to court (article by O. Sulaimonova and J. Rasulova).
Third-party monitoring and ILO results
Since 2013, a practice of monitoring child and forced labor with the participation of
ILO experts has been in effect (the ”Third-party Monitoring” project). According to
the results of 2013, the ILO concluded that child labor in cotton harvesting was not
used systematically, although cases of forced labor were recognized. Independent
monitoring for 2014–2018 concluded: systematic use of child labor has been elimi-
nated, and in 2019 this issue ”is no longer on the agenda.” The national monitoring
of the 2019 cotton campaign was conducted for the first time with the participation
of US trade unions and European trade union centers under the coordination of the
International Trade Union Confederation (article by O. Sulaimonova and J. Rasulova).
Cotton monoculture: historical roots
B. A. Bhat shows: child labor was preceded by the history of cotton monoculture. By
1911-12, Turkestan already supplied 52% of the needs of the Russian textile indus-
try, and by 1914–15 — 70%; cotton plantations between 1886 and 1900 grew from
41,000 to 92,888 dessiatines, and the railway that came to Tashkent in 1898 ”opened
Central Asia to Russian capital.” Uzbekistan is the second largest producer and ex-
porter of cotton in the world (over 800,000 tons annually), providing about 60% of
Central Asia’s cotton: 3.5–3.7 million tons of raw material and 1–1.2 million tons of
fiber per year. For irrigation of 1.47 million hectares under cotton, the regime al-
most destroyed the Aral Sea — once the fourth-largest lake in the world, which has
retained only 15% of its former volume and lost 24 species of endemic fish (article
by B. A. Bhat).
Child labor in cotton: scale and conditions
During the harvest, schools were closed for two to three months, and children from
the age of seven were sent to the fields — first 15–16-year-olds, then 12–14-year-olds,
and by the end of September even first-graders. According to EJF, in the Fergana
Valley, about 200,000 children worked annually; according to UNICEF (2000), 22.6%
of children aged 5–14 worked at least part-time. The workday lasted 10–12 hours
(from 6:30–7:00 AM to 7:00–7:30 PM; home by 9:00–10:00 PM) in heat up to 45 °C,
without shade or protection; children drank water from irrigation canals, lived in
barracks without windows and doors. Payment was from $5 for five days to 15 cents;
according to the NGO ”Tahlil” (2001), a kilogram of cotton cost from 1.5 to 1 cent,
while on the world market it was $1.15. Over two years in the Samarkand region,
the deaths of eight children were recorded (article by B. A. Bhat).
Causes, educational losses, and state response
According to the ILRF study ”We Live Subject to Their Orders” (2008), the roots of
forced child labor are not poverty or tradition, but the nature of the state and control
over rural society: a command economy with quotas and demechanization (machine
harvesting fell from two-thirds to 10%) require coercion; the mobilization of children
14


History of Uzbekistan · Weeks 5–6
·
through schools is organized by khokimiats. Two months of school closures mean a
loss of over 20% of instructional time; for grades 5–9, losses accumulate to a full
academic year. The state responded: in 2001, cotton harvesting was included in the
list of worst forms of child labor; in March 2008, the parliament pledged to ratify
conventions No. 182 and No. 138 (ratified in March 2008 and March 2009). The
2007 Law ”On Guarantees of the Child’s Right to Labor” permits work from age
16, from 15 with written parental consent, and from 14 light work outside of school
(article by B. A. Bhat).
3.2 3.2. Questions — Article Questions and Model Answers
S1. How does ILO Convention No. 29 define forced labor?
Answer. ”Forced or compulsory labor means all work or service which is exacted from
any person under the threat of any penalty and to which he has not offered himself
voluntarily.” The definition rests on four elements: work or service; any person (adult
or child, citizen or migrant); involuntary nature; threat of punishment, which may
not be criminal — for example, loss of rights or privileges. Art. 2 of the Convention
does not extend the concept to military service, ordinary civic obligations, work done
under sentence of a court, emergencies, and minor communal works (article by O.
Sulaimanova and J. Rasulov).
S2. In what five cases does Convention No. 105 require the immediate ces-
sation of forced labor?
Answer. As a means of political coercion or education or as punishment for political
opinions; as a method of mobilizing and using labor for economic development; as
a means of ensuring labor discipline; as punishment for participation in strikes; as
a means of racial, social, national or religious discrimination. Whereas Convention
No.
29 prohibits forced labor in general (with exceptions), No.
105 requires its
immediate cessation in these five cases (article by O. Sulaimanova and J. Rasulov).
S3. Which ILO conventions has Uzbekistan ratified?
Answer. As of January 1, 2021 — 17 conventions (including 8 fundamental ones) and
1 protocol: conventions No. 29 (1930) and No. 105 (1957) on forced labor, No. 182
(1999) on the worst forms of child labor, No. 138 (1973) on minimum age, and the
2014 Protocol to Convention No. 29 (ratified on June 25, 2019, entered into force for
Uzbekistan on September 16, 2020). The 1966 UN Covenants have also been ratified.
The first period of institutional development (1992–2007) began with joining the ILO
and ratifying conventions No.
29 and No.
105 (article by O. Sulaimanova and J.
Rasulov).
S4.
Why is ratification of conventions ”50 percent of the solution to the
problem”?
Answer. This was stated by T. Narbaeva, who headed the Uzbekistan delegation at
the 103rd session of the International Labour Conference: ratification is only half
the battle; the rest is the implementation of international norms into national legis-
lation, and most importantly, changing law enforcement practices and the mindset
of the population, especially farmers and employers. The authors confirm: in the his-
tory of the ILO, there have been many cases when a state ratified a convention and
considered its obligations fulfilled, while I supervisory bodies since the 1930s have
emphasized the insufficiency of ratification alone (article by O. Sulaimanova and J.
Rasulov).
S5. How does national legislation define forced labor and what are its short-
comings?
15

History of Uzbekistan · Weeks 5–6
·
Answer. Art. 7 of the Labor Code (developing Art. 37 of the Constitution) prohibits
”the performance of work under the threat of any penalty (including as a means of
maintaining labor discipline).” Shortcomings: the element of voluntary non-offering
of services has been excluded from the definition; forced labor is limited to the sphere
of labor law, whereas Convention No. 29 applies outside of labor relations as well; the
phrase ”in other cases provided for by law” conflicts with the closed list of exceptions
in the Convention. Art. 1482 of the Criminal Code and Art. 51 of the Administrative
Code only punish ”administrative coercion” to labor (article by O. Sulaimanova and
J. Rasulov).
S6. What is hashar and when is it not considered forced labor?
Answer. Hashar is ”voluntary, disinterested participation of the majority in carrying
out a task” (dictionary definition). According to the Government’s resolution No. 349
of May 10, 2018, mandatory involvement in public works, including construction
and agricultural, is allowed only on a voluntary basis and with the presence of a
Presidential decree or a Government resolution; without strict permission, greening
and improvement can be organized. The key factor is good will: coercion to hashar
under the threat of punishment is forced labor. The authors propose to enshrine the
definition of hashar in law (article by O. Sulaimanova and J. Rasulov).
S7. What three periods of formation of mechanisms against forced labor do
the authors identify?
Answer. (1) 1992–2007 — ratification of conventions No. 29 and No. 105, joining the
ILO, adoption of the Labor Code and the Employment Law, creation of labor inspec-
tions; no specialized structures yet. (2) 2008–2016 — international claims, national
action plans, first anti-trafficking institutions: Law ”On Counteracting Trafficking in
Persons”, resolutions No. 207, No. 82, No. 132, commissions, Rehabilitation Cen-
ter, Coordination Council on Child Labor (2013). (3) Since 2017 — criminal liability,
new mechanisms, resumption of cooperation with the ILO, positive conclusions from
international organizations (article by O. Sulyaimanova and J. Rasulov).
S8. What bodies are combating forced labor today?
Answer. Three types of mechanisms: collegial — National Commission on Combating
Trafficking in Persons and Forced Labor (decree PF-5775 of July 30, 2019), Coordi-
nation Council on Child Labor, Republican Trilateral Commission on Social and La-
bor Issues; labor — state labor inspections, authorized to initiate cases and transfer
materials to courts; public — trade unions and NGOs participating in tripartite nego-
tiations and monitoring. The institution of the national rapporteur annually reports
to the President on the situation with forced labor (article by O. Sulyaimanova and
J. Rasulov).
S9. What results did the 2019–2020 monitoring show?
Answer. In 2019, 259 cases of forced labor were identified (141 — in cotton harvest-
ing), fines amounting to 772 million soms were imposed under Art. 51 of the Code of
Administrative Offenses. For the 2020 cotton campaign, 42 officials, including heads
of organizations, khokims and their deputies, were held administratively liable; in 6
cases, documents were transferred to court. Cluster and farm managers were also
held liable: 61 cases of failure to conclude labor contracts, 34 — failure to provide
working conditions, 13 — failure to fulfill obligations, 17 — untimely payment of
wages (article by O. Sulyaimanova and J. Rasulov).
S10. What did the ILO’s third-party monitoring establish?
Answer. Since 2013, monitoring of child and forced labor with the participation of
ILO experts and human rights defenders has been practiced. Result of 2013: child
16


History of Uzbekistan · Weeks 5–6
·
labor in cotton harvesting does not have a systematic nature, although there are
cases of forced labor. Independent monitoring of 2014–2018: systematic use of child
labor has been eliminated; in 2019, the issue was no longer on the agenda, significant
progress was noted in the fight against forced labor. In the 2019 national monitoring,
US and European trade unions participated for the first time under the coordination
of the International Confederation of Trade Unions (article by O. Sulyaimanova and
J. Rasulov).
S11. Why did child labor become mass-scale in Uzbekistan’s cotton industry?
Answer. B. A. Bhat links this to the command economy: state quotas push production
above the market-determined level, lack of market incentives requires coercion, and
demechanization (machine harvesting fell from two-thirds in Soviet times to 10%)
increased the need for cheap labor. ILRF research (2008) showed that the reasons
are not poverty or tradition, but the nature of the state and control over rural society:
khokimiyats organize the mobilization of children through schools, passing down
quotas down to the individual child. Without agrarian sector reform, the problem
cannot be solved (article by B. A. Bhat).
S12. What were the scale and conditions of child labor in cotton?
Answer. According to EJF, about 200,000 children worked annually in the Fergana
Valley; according to UNICEF (2000), 22.6% of children aged 5–14 worked at least
part-time. Schools were closed for two to three months, children worked 10–12 hours
a day in heat up to 45 °C, drank water from irrigation canals, lived in barracks without
electricity, windows, or doors. Payment — from $5 for five days to 15 cents; according
to the NGO ”Tahlil” (2001), a kilogram of cotton cost from 1.5 to 1 cent, while on the
world market it was $1.15. Over two years in the Samarkand region, the deaths of
eight children were recorded (article by B. A. Bhat).
S13. How did child labor affect education?
Answer. The two-month closure of schools is effectively subtracted from learning:
the net loss is over 20% of instructional time, and accumulated losses from grades 5
to 9 reach a full academic year. In the spring, children were additionally mobilized for
weeding, thinning, and transplanting seedlings—classes were suspended for weeks.
Parents and teachers acknowledge that education is suffering; rural children find
themselves in an unequal position compared to urban children and are aware of the
losses for their future prospects. Bhat calls for reliable data and methodologically
sound monitoring tools (article by B. A. Bhat).
S14. How did the state and law respond to the problem of child labor?
Answer. As early as 2001, the ministries of education and labor included manual
cotton picking in the list of the worst forms of child labor; the UN Committee on the
Rights of the expressed ”deep concern” over the involvement of schoolchildren in
harvesting. In March 2008, the parliament pledged to ratify conventions No. 182
and No.
138 (ratified in March 2008 and March 2009), and in September 2008,
a national action plan was adopted. The 2007 Law ”On Guarantees of the Child’s
Right to Labor” permits employment from age 16, from age 15 with written parental
consent, and from age 14 with light work outside of school; Art. 241 of the Labor
Code prohibits work harmful to health and morality (article by B. A. Bhat).
